facts.text: Experts disagree on whether the UN R152 virtual testing provisions proposed by industry associations are credible enough: the United Kingdom's GRVA-18-55 (January 2024) argued for physical testing evidenced for every toolchain component, while the Russian Federation (November 2025) argued for mandatory physical verification of the virtual model.
facts.quote: physical testing "should be used and evidenced for all the components of the toolchain", and the Russian Federation (November 2025) argued for mandatory physical verification of the virtual model; industry associations proposed the provisions.

facts.text: The 30% physical-test share stated in the UTAC CERAM working document and vendor commentary cannot be reconciled with the adopted WP.29 text for UN R152, which leaves the number of physical confirmatory tests to agreement between manufacturer and authority. The adopted text governs.
facts.quote: The 30% figure in the UTAC CERAM working document and the vendor commentary cannot be reconciled with the adopted WP.29 text, which leaves the number of physical confirmatory tests to agreement between manufacturer and authority; the adopted text governs.

facts.text: Experts disagree on how far similarity and analysis may replace large physical tests: proponents emphasize validated-family reuse and efficiency, while skeptics emphasize that apparently minor design details can change failure mechanisms.
facts.quote: Proponents emphasize validated-family reuse and efficiency; skeptics emphasize apparently minor design details that change failure mechanisms.

facts.text: The FAA Transport Airplane Crashworthiness and Ditching Working Group record of 15 December 2017 includes a DLR dissent against replacing large physical tests through similarity and design review: DLR argued that these approaches could be unsafe for some composite crash structures and that at least one large structural test should remain.
facts.quote: The FAA Transport Airplane Crashworthiness and Ditching Working Group record (15 December 2017) includes a DLR dissent arguing that similarity and design-review approaches could be unsafe for some composite crash structures and that at least one large structural test should remain.

facts.text: Experts disagree on whether the area validation metric is a sound acceptance criterion: the concern challenging its soundness is that greater experimental scatter can make a model look better.
facts.quote: Whether the area validation metric is a sound acceptance criterion**, given that more experimental scatter can make a model look better.

facts.text: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board viewed Columbia as a model-validity failure, whereas Hale viewed Columbia as a management override of a correct warning.
facts.quote: Whether Columbia was a model-validity failure** (the Board's view) **or a management override of a correct warning** (Hale).

facts.text: NASA deliberately avoids aggregating credibility into a single score, whereas engineering organizations often want dashboards or maturity scores. For a safety board, the passage favors NASA's position of preserving credibility dimensions and their evidence so that a high score in one area cannot invisibly compensate for weak validation in another.
facts.quote: For a safety board the NASA position is more defensible: preserve the dimensions and their evidence rather than let a high score in one area compensate invisibly for weak validation in another.

facts.text: Experts disagree on how far PIRT-style subjective ranking is acceptable without explicitly treating its subjectivity; the disputed positions concern accepting subjective ranking versus requiring explicit treatment of that subjectivity.
facts.quote: How far PIRT-style subjective ranking is acceptable** without explicit treatment of the subjectivity.
